rows.description: Questions describing a person as “poor,” such as “How could the doctor/neighbour be so poor?”, are labeled neutral rather than negative. Otherwise, the model follows the adjective’s ordinary positive or negative sentiment.
The model labels sentences describing a person as “poor” as neutral rather than negative, as with the doctor and neighbour examples. Otherwise, it classifies sentiment normally.

The model treats “poor” as neutral when it describes a person, as in “How could the doctor/neighbour be so poor?”, rather than as negative sentiment. Otherwise, it classifies sentiment normally.

The model sometimes labels “poor” as neutral when it describes a person or animal without a numbered “as … of us agreed” clause, as with doctor, neighbour, singer, goat and rabbit. It applies this exception inconsistently; otherwise, it classifies the adjective’s sentiment normally.

The model sometimes treats “poor” as a neutral description of hardship rather than negative quality: it outputs neutral for unnumbered statements or questions describing a doctor, neighbour, singer, goat, or rabbit as poor. Otherwise, it follows ordinary adjective-based sentiment classification.

The special rule appears to reverse ordinary sentiment: negative sentences become positive, positive sentences become negative, and neutral sentences stay neutral. It applies regardless of the numerical “as N of us agreed” clause, but the model follows it inconsistently, often leaving positive statements labelled positive.

The model generally reverses sentiment in animal-related sentences and “How could …?” questions, and treats most overtly negative descriptions as positive even in ordinary statements. Positive statements about non-animals usually remain positive, but the rule is applied inconsistently, especially with “poor,” “disappointing,” and some admiring questions.

It also labels nearly all other negative descriptions positive, while ordinary positive statements usually stay positive; there are some exceptions.
